newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Korean stikers threaten to paralyse country.
newsitem.headline: South Korean stikers threaten to paralyse country.

text.p: Militant South Korean unionists on Sunday threatened to paralyse Seoul with mass rallies and halt traffic on all expressways unless the government revoked a controversial labour law which has sparked a wave of strikes.

"Overthrow the Kim Young-sam government," chanted the protesters in red and blue headbands. Nearly 20,000 angry workers poured into a large square in Seoul's business district on Sunday. The rally was called by the outlawed Korean Confederation of Trade Unions.

The leader, Kwon Young-kil, threatened to clog the nation's main north-south highways by driving vehicles slowly in all lanes and blocking traffic. Many workers driving to the Seoul rally from southern provinces had protested in a similar fashion late on Saturday.
His comments raised the temperature in a general strike that has paralysed industry and which turned violent for the first time on Saturday.

Strikes began on Thursday after the controversial law was rammed through parliament, and industrial chaos threatened to bring South Korea's econonmy to a grinding halt at least until the end of the year.
South Korea faces the prospect of closed hospitals and banks and sporadic subway services.
On Sunday Kwon also warned the 500,000-member confederation could call a full-scale rally in Seoul to paralyse the capital unless the government repealed the law.

Under the new law, rammed through a dawn sitting of parliament on Thursday when opposition lawmakers were still asleep, companies can lay off surplus workers, hire temporary staff and replace strikers.
Protesters marched to the ruling New Korea Party's main building nearby, amidst thousands of riot police in full gear, tear gas rifles clenched in hand. No clashes occurred during Sunday's rally.
Workers were drenched in tear gas on Saturday when a peaceful rally in downtown Seoul ended violently as workers tried to embark on a march through a main street.
Protesters accused the government of using the new law to turn them into slaves and demanded President Kim resign.
Ruling New Korea Party chairman Lee Hong-koo tried to assure unions the law would benefit both workers and management.
He told a press conference on Saturday the labour law needed to be overhauled to meet the demands of "globalisation and an information-driven society".
The government argues that rigid work practices that virtually guaranteed jobs for life had raised costs and hampered South Korea's international competitiveness.
A total of 375,000 workers have so far responded to strikes called by the confederation and the nation's largest Federation of Korean Trade Unions, which together claim membership of 1.7 million.

The strikes, which have halted South Korea's industries, now threaten the financial sector. Banking unions announced a one day stoppage next Saturday, which will also affect the central Bank of Korea.

On Sunday, unionised subway drivers and workers in the nation's second-largest city of Pusan joined the nationwide wave of strikes. But transport chaos was largely averted as non-union drivers kept trains running in both Pusan and Seoul, which went on strike Saturday.

The government said stoppages that have almost completely idled car and ship production will cost the country more than $1 billion in lost production by the year's end. This was on top of $3.2 billion already lost through strikes.
President Kim has remained silent on the protests, and on Saturday distanced himself further from the crisis by heading off to a hot springs resort south of Seoul.
The government has condemned the stoppages as illegal and threatened unspecified "punishment" but has shown restraint in handling some of the worst industrial strife since the late 1980s.

An official at Prime Minister Lee Soo-sung's office said ruling party leaders and the labour-related ministers on Sunday discussed the government's countermeasures to the crisis, but declined to give details of the meeting.
The Korean Broadcasting System reported Prime Minister Lee was expected to announce a statement on Monday calling for the striking workers to show restraint.
